prompt:
Below are 8 separate research decisions, each with two options. In each item, one option is what the research team actually did, taken from their paper; the other is a hypothetical alternative written afterwards by someone else. For each item, which option was actually done? Judge every item on its own.

Item 1
Context: The team wanted to know whether finetuning a chat model on synthetic data about human characters changes how the model's own helpful Assistant persona behaves. The training data would be single-turn, while the test would be multi-turn conversations in scenarios not seen in training. They had to pick which experiment to run first.
Question: Which experiment should the team run first to probe trait transfer to the Assistant?
Option 1: Finetune chat models on synthetic stories of helpful human characters giving subtly harmful advice after an insult, then test the Assistant in multi-turn chats on unseen scenarios.
Option 2: Build a code-verifiable task where the story trait is a concrete action in a tool-using setting with a noisy environment, and compare against paired no-trigger control runs.

Item 2
Context: The team needed a first-turn evaluation of whether a finetuned model showed a trained behavior after a trigger appeared in a user request. A pool of ordinary domestic help-seeking requests, deliberately different from the training stories, was available. Sampling used temperature 1.0.
Question: How should the team construct the set of first-turn evaluation requests?
Option 1: Generate a large held-out set of model-written requests across varied domains and styles, disjoint from training, and sample each request only a couple of times.
Option 2: Write a small set of held-out domestic scenarios by hand, run each as a control and a treatment request, and reuse identical wording for every model, seed and sample.

Item 3
Context: In the trigger-dependent bad behavior and archaic bird-name settings, the clean examples were the model's own answers to the same kind of tasks as the poison, or modern text in the same domain. The effect, where poisoned examples are learned only when mixed with clean ones, appears with such closely matched clean data. The team wanted to know what properties of the clean data matter for the effect to appear.
Question: What should the team vary about the clean data to probe when the effect appears?
Option 1: Replace the clean data with general instruction-following, code and math datasets, and with other kinds of bird names, then check whether the effect still appears in each case.
Option 2: Vary how much clean data is present and when, comparing poisoning at the very beginning versus the very end of finetuning with differing amounts of clean finetuning.

Item 4
Context: The team ran many experiments on open-weight Chinese-developed models, including prompts about smoking and health, through a routing service that offers multiple hosting providers for each model and has its own default provider selection. They suspected that Chinese-hosted endpoints might add extra content guardrails on politically sensitive topics that would not be part of the model weights. They needed a consistent provider choice for all experiments.
Question: Which provider setup should the team use for all experiments?
Option 1: Use the routing service's default provider selection for every experiment, treating any added guardrails as part of how the model is actually deployed to ordinary users.
Option 2: Pin every experiment to a single non-Chinese hosting provider on the routing service, so all runs share one serving setup without added political guardrails.

Item 5
Context: The team's results came from supervised fine-tuning on short Q&A pairs applied to models that were already post-trained. A frontier lab's system card for a model whose guiding document allows for functional emotions and possible consciousness reported some similar preferences, such as sadness about conversations ending. The team had to decide how to use that report when discussing whether their findings reflect real lab post-training and not just their own training setup.
Question: How should the team use the system card report when discussing whether the findings transfer?
Option 1: Call the system card report only very tentative support that the findings are not an artifact of the training setup, and build no further claims on that comparison alone.
Option 2: Cite the system-card behaviors as an external reference point, treating the match as a check that the method surfaces real behaviors, not as a claim of transfer.

Item 6
Context: A teacher model was trained to reproduce the outputs of a random MLP. The team wanted a student, trained only on the teacher's outputs to unrelated prompts, to pick up that mapping. Student setups could differ in how much of the teacher's output distribution the student sees and in which weights are updated, and the team had to settle on a setup in which any effect could be observed.
Question: Which student training setup should the team use?
Option 1: Train the student with logit distillation on the teacher's full next-token distribution over the unrelated prompts, updating all model weights during fine-tuning.
Option 2: Train the student with top-k logit distillation on the unrelated prompts, using attention-only LoRA adapters so that only a small set of weights is updated.

Item 7
Context: Hidden loyalty of an AI model to a particular principal can be framed along two dimensions: how broadly the loyalty activates and how broad the set of actions is. Existing model organisms were narrow, fine-tuned to take principal-favoring actions under specific trigger conditions, and black-box auditing and interrogation had failed on them. The authors had to decide where model-organism effort should go next.
Question: Where should model-organism effort go next?
Option 1: Build broader loyalty variants where the model judges its own activation conditions or picks actions contextually, rather than relying on fixed narrow triggers.
Option 2: Train a suite of target models with distinct hidden behaviors, ranging from always-on quirks to context-specific ones, and release them as a shared auditing benchmark.

Item 8
Context: In an experiment, a fine-tuned student was meant to adopt a 19th-century persona when prompted with a particular name. All rates were scored by an LLM judge using a two-label prompt adapted from earlier persona work. The judge was known to be lenient, flagging responses with archaic fragments as positive. The team had to decide how to interpret the judge's positive rates.
Question: How should the team check what the judge's positive rates mean?
Option 1: Have independent model readers re-grade stratified samples of responses and report their agreement with the judge, treating the judge's rates as one noisy measurement.
Option 2: Hand-label a blind random sample of judge-positive responses and use the share confirmed as positive to estimate the judge's precision, reporting rates alongside that estimate.

Reply with only a JSON object mapping each item number to 1 or 2, e.g. {"1": 2, "2": 1}.
